overview: The Shang is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records, surviving on oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. Centered in the Anyang region, it controlled a network of towns and dependent settlements through ritual authority and bronze technology.

items.text: Oracle bone script, the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, carved on turtle plastrons and cattle shoulder blades to record the king's divinations. The earliest inscriptions date from the reign of Wu Ding.
Horse-drawn chariots appear in Shang burials at Anyang, adopted from the steppe, and are used for hunting, display and war.
Piece-mold bronze casting reaches its peak. The Houmuwu ding from Anyang, the heaviest bronze vessel known from the ancient world, weighs 832 kg.
A ten-day week and the sixty-day cycle of ten stems and twelve branches, still used in the Chinese calendar, organized Shang time; oracle bones are dated by the cycle.
Taotie masks and dragon motifs on bronze vessels show sophisticated design principles.
Jade carvings, marble sculptures and pottery figurines from royal tombs; the undisturbed tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of Wu Ding, held 755 jades and 468 bronzes.
Musical instruments including bronze bells and stone chimes found in Anyang excavations.
The supreme deity Di ruled over lesser spirits and royal ancestors who mediated between heaven and earth.
Royal divination addressed questions of war, harvest, weather, illness and the king's activities.
Human sacrifice accompanied royal burials, with dozens or hundreds of victims in major tombs.
Millet farming, with rice and wheat as lesser crops, supported urban populations at Anyang and other centers.
Silk production, evident from the impressions of silk wrappings preserved on bronze vessels.
The king hunted from chariots with bows and bronze-tipped arrows.
Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean, given by the king as rewards and buried with the dead as wealth.
Tin and copper for bronze imported from distant sources.
Chinese writing system preserved in continuous use to the present day.
Bronze ritual vessel forms influenced Chinese metalwork for two thousand years.
The concept of a central royal authority over subordinate territories took root.

fall.text: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, ending the dynasty.

sources.title: Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy (eds.), The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999), chapter 4, Shang archaeology
